question: What is the main building role of lipids in our bodies?

options.A: Building the outer layer of every cell
options.B: Acting as enzymes to speed up reactions
options.C: Providing quick energy for the brain
options.D: Carrying water-soluble vitamins in the blood

explanation: You've got this! Phospholipids and cholesterol act like tiny bricks that form the protective wall (membrane) around all our cells. Great job! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h1)

question: Why do we actually need dietary fats to absorb certain vitamins?

options.A: Fat binds directly to water-soluble vitamins
options.B: Fat makes the stomach produce more acid
options.C: Vitamins A, D, E, and K dissolve in fat
options.D: Fat stops the liver from destroying vitamins

explanation: Think of fat as the vehicle that carries vitamins A, D, E, and K through your gut so your body can use them. Without fat, these vitamins just pass right through! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h1)

question: What chemical feature makes a fatty acid 'saturated'?

options.A: It only comes from plant sources
options.B: It stays completely liquid at room temperature
options.C: It has no double bonds between carbon atoms
options.D: It has multiple double bonds in the chain

explanation: Saturated fats are packed tightly together with single bonds only, which is why butter (a saturated fat) stays solid at room temperature! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h2)

question: A patient with high cholesterol asks which fat to avoid completely. What should you tell them?
explanation: Trans fats are artificial troublemakers! They raise bad cholesterol and lower the good kind, so it's best to avoid them for a healthy heart. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h2)

question: What is the recommended daily percentage range for total fat intake in healthy adults?
explanation: Aiming for 20% to 35% of daily calories from fats keeps adults energized and healthy without overdoing it. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h3)

question: Why do health guidelines look closely at the *type* of fat we eat, rather than just total grams?

options.A: The body cannot digest saturated fats at all
options.C: Different fats have very different effects on heart health
options.D: Total fat intake has no effect on body weight

explanation: Not all fats are enemies! While trans fats clog arteries, healthy fats like olive oil protect your heart. It's all about quality over quantity. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h3)

question: What is a common long-term effect of eating too many trans and saturated fats?

options.B: Stronger storage of vitamins in bones

explanation: Eating too many bad fats causes fatty plaque to build up in the arteries (atherosclerosis), making the heart work much harder. Good catch! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h4)

question: Which problem is most likely to happen if someone has a severe lack of dietary fat?

options.B: Trouble absorbing vitamins A, D, E, and K
options.D: Too much good cholesterol in the blood

explanation: Remember, fat-soluble vitamins need dietary fat to get absorbed! Without enough fat, deficiency symptoms start to show up. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h4)

question: A patient with high cholesterol uses butter for all their cooking. What heart-healthy swap can you suggest?
explanation: Liquid plant oils like olive or canola are rich in unsaturated fats, making them fantastic, heart-friendly swaps for solid butter! [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h5)

question: Why is teaching patients to read food labels a great nursing skill for fat management?

options.A: It proves processed foods are dangerous
options.B: It helps them spot hidden trans and saturated fats
options.D: It means they never need to see a dietitian again

explanation: Food labels can be tricky! Teaching patients to read them empowers them to catch hidden bad fats lurking in packaged snacks. [learn more](GNS227_U4_T011#GNS227_U4_T011_h5)
